sometimes adverb

also now and then, at times, occasionally, sometimes … sometimes, from time to time

classical

Cic. Off. 2.64: sed interdum etiam frūctuōsum
Mor. 28: interdum fessae succēdit laeva sorōrī
Traupman 40
Traupman 311
Traupman 382, 394

interdum

adverb

sometimes, now and then

Other words

  • nōnnumquam (nōn numquam) — sometimes, not never

    adverb · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.8.4: nōn numquam interdiū, saepius noctū; Quint. 1.5.58: sīcut illī ā nōbīs nōnnumquam mūtuantur; Traupman 382

  • 1aliquandō: long final o (Lewis & Short aliquandŏ). A compound of quandō, which de Vaan gives with a long final vowel (p. 507, s.v. quī); Festus records an older form quandōd (Lewis & Short s.v. quando). The Latinitas loci write aliquandō throughout, and the house quandō.

    aliquandō1 — sometimes, now and then (as against never)

    adverb · also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 83.6: aliquandō dormīsse mē sciō, aliquandō suspicor; Plin. Ep. 9.36.6: vēnor aliquandō

  • modo … modo — sometimes … sometimes, now … now

    also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 713: modo ait, modo negat; Traupman 382

  • per occāsiōnem — when the chance offers (not “occasionally”)

    avoid · classical · Liv. 1.5.5: rem inmātūram nisi per occāsiōnem aperīre nōluerat (Lewis & Short); Traupman 41

    Traupman gives per occāsiōnem for “occasionally”; classically it means “on a favourable opportunity” (Lewis & Short). For “occasionally” use interdum or nōnnumquam.

Examples

  • est enim nōn modo līberāle paulum nōn numquam dē suō jūre dēcēdere, sed interdum etiam frūctuōsum

    for to give up a little of your rights now and then is not only generous but sometimes even profitableCic. Off. 2.64

  • aliquandō dormīsse mē sciō, aliquandō suspicor

    sometimes I know I’ve slept, sometimes I only suspect itSen. Ep. 83.6

  • modo ait, modo negat

    sometimes he says yes, sometimes noTer. Eun. 713

See also ever, once.
